COMMON GOOD AND MY GOOD - CHAPTER OVERVIEW
- Opening quote: "No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends." (John 15:13)
- Irish proverb at the start: "Ar scath a cheile a mhaireann na daoine" (people live in each other's shelter).
- The chapter covers: personal and community values; when values clash; balancing values; the common good (Higher Level only from that point on); definitions from Greece, Rome and Christianity; Vatican II; a universal common good; challenges (diversity/pluralism, decline of civic spirit, utilitarianism); Irish civil law and the common good with three court cases.

PERSONAL VALUES
- Value: a desired quality that we consider good and important.
- Examples of personal values:
- Sheila values her health: she had a health scare years ago and now has a young family.
- Dmitri loves his freedom: he grew up in relative poverty and oppression in Eastern Europe and now in the West can live as he wishes.
- Hugh is driven by a sense of social justice: his aunts worked on the missions in Africa and showed him the injustice and corruption in the world.
- Other things people value: personal fulfilment, happy family life, interesting work, a good standard of living, quality leisure time.
- Our values are shaped by the type of person we are, how we were brought up and educated, and our experiences.

COMMUNITY VALUES
- A community can be any grouping: a family, a team, a town, a country, a church. Any community can have an agreed, common value.
- Examples:
- A family values togetherness, so everyone meets for Sunday dinner.
- Trocaire values justice for all, especially those suffering from oppression.
- The Irish State values the right of all to an education, according to the Constitution, and pledges to protect it.
- Community value: a value that seeks the good not just of an individual but of the whole community; a good for all people in that community.
- Often our personal values are the same as those needed for the good of the whole community.
- Charters that present community values: the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights and the Ten Commandments (Decalogue). It is challenging to agree these values in the modern world.

WHEN VALUES COLLIDE
- People live out of different value systems; even people in the same classroom hold different values.
- What is good for me and good for the community may not be the same.
- Examples of conflicting values:
- Some Jehovah's Witnesses do not allow blood transfusions for religious reasons. If a child needs a transfusion, should the hospital treat the child or respect the parents' right to act on their beliefs?
- A company wants to build an incinerator: it would give jobs and deal with waste from unsightly landfills, but the local community campaigns against it because of health concerns.
- Fiona values her fitness to get on the school basketball team, but her friends smoke and drink at weekends; she doesn't want to miss out on her friends.

BALANCING VALUES
- With conflicting social values, a balance has to be achieved.
- The State's duty to protect the health of the nation is balanced with people's right to choose how they live.
- Example: hundreds die in car accidents each year, but the State will not ban driving, because people have a right to travel and banning cars would harm the progress of society.
- Personal freedoms must be balanced with the overall good of society:
- People are free to make as much money as they can, but must pay taxes so social services can be provided for all.
- People are free to listen to any music, but should not disturb neighbours at night. Civil law balances one person's right to party with another's right to sleep.

COMMON GOOD AND INDIVIDUAL RIGHTS (HIGHER LEVEL ONLY FROM HERE)
- Bhutan, a small country between India and Burma, usually ranked last in FIFA world soccer rankings. Its Prime Minister said GNH (gross national happiness) is more important than GNP (gross national product).
- Irish Times headline, 30 June 2005: "It's official: Irish more satisfied with their lot than the average European".
- Desert island 'values' exercise: choose five of ten people (armed police officer, David Beckham, an eighty-year-old rabbi, a doctor with HIV/AIDS, her husband, her five-year-old daughter, Kerry footballer Seamus Moynihan, An Taoiseach, Cameron Diaz, a fisherman who speaks no English) and say what value each represents and offers the community.

WHAT IS THE COMMON GOOD?
- The Common Good: a concept discussed throughout history by thinkers of all beliefs.
- Common: shared by everyone in the community.
- Good: a goal that is sought for fulfilment.
- It is an attempt to define what is best for the whole of society.
- It seeks to foster ways of cooperating so that shared objectives are achieved for the fulfilment of all the people.
- It is generally seen as a counter-balance to excessive individualism.
- Sometimes what is good for the community is not good for the person, and vice versa.

DEFINITIONS: GREECE AND ROME
- Plato (The Republic): "The goal of the ideal state is not the advantage of any one class but the greatest possible happiness of the city as a whole."
- Example: a fair tax system serves the common good because sharing wealth contributes to the greatest happiness of all.
- Classical Greece saw the polis (city state) as the place of human flourishing. The individual was private and incomplete. The State was more important than the person.
- Aristotle: the human person is by nature a social and political being whose happiness is achieved through the public virtues of citizenship.
- Aristotle (Politics): "Political society exists for the sake of noble actions, and not of mere companionship." So seeking the common good brings about one's own happiness.
- Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics): "Even if the good is the same for the individual and the city, the good of the city clearly is the greater and more perfect thing to attain and to safeguard... to secure it for a nation and for cities is nobler and more divine."
- Cicero (106-43 BCE), Rome: a commonwealth (res publica: republic) is an "assemblage of people in large numbers associated in agreement with respect to justice and a partnership for the common good."
- The idea is found in the political tradition of republicanism and in the writings of Machiavelli and Rousseau.

CHRISTIANITY AND THE COMMON GOOD
- The command to love one's neighbour as oneself demands a commitment to the common good.
- Christianity adds that the final good of every person is in following God's plan. Politics and economics can achieve much, but complete happiness and fulfilment is with God.
- This gives a religious motivation for seeking the common good and reminds believers their final destiny is in God's hands, not the State's - a different emphasis from Greece and Rome.
- Christianity rejects the extreme of INDIVIDUALISM (selfishness and lack of care for others), because we are called to live in community and love our neighbour.
- It also rejects TOTALITARIANISM, which puts the good of the State above the good of the person (e.g. Nazi Germany).
- A person's freedom and dignity are achieved in communion with others, not in isolation.

VATICAN II AND CATHOLIC SOCIAL TEACHING
- Catholic social teaching: the Church's teaching on issues that affect society, based on the principles of human dignity and solidarity.
- At the Second Vatican Council (1960s) the Church spoke of people becoming more selfish and of the need to serve the common good.
- Gaudium et spes 30 (adapted):
- No one can "close their eyes to the course of events" or "wallow in the luxury of a merely individualistic morality".
- "The best way to fulfil one's obligations of justice and love is to contribute to the common good according to one's means and the needs of others."
- Some "boast of grand and noble sentiments but live in practice as if they did not care about the need of society".
- Blocks to the common good named: people who use fraud and cheating to avoid paying just taxes and social obligations; people who neglect norms of social conduct such as public hygiene and speed limits, endangering their own and others' lives.
- "Let everyone consider it their sacred duty to count social obligations among their chief duties today."
- Summary: the classical Catholic concept of the common good now has two complementary interpretations:
- It must allow for full participation of everyone.
- It must include respect for personal rights and duties.

A UNIVERSAL COMMON GOOD
- The world is becoming smaller (Internet, text-messaging).
- Alliances such as the European Union and the United Nations work together for the common good of humanity.
- The common good is no longer protected only by individual states; it is the duty of the whole world community.
- Examples: ensuring fair trade, protecting the environment, responding to humanitarian crises of famine and refugees.
- Organisations: UN bodies (e.g. food organisation, High Commission for Refugees), Concern, Trocaire, Amnesty International.

CHALLENGES TO THE COMMON GOOD: DIVERSITY
- Can everyone agree on what the common good is?
- John Rawls says it is impossible to agree on a common good when so many different goods are sought in society.
- Pluralism: the existence of many different beliefs in one society (covered more in the next chapter). Diversity can make life interesting or be a source of fear, but it makes a shared vision harder.
- Some feel that in a pluralist society the only shared vision is tolerance of every vision - respect for the person is taken as more important than the common good for all.
- Others feel diversity helps us become more conscious of what really binds us together as a community.
- "We can know a good in common that we cannot know alone." Example: the Man/Woman of the Match saying "It was really a team effort".

CHALLENGES: DECLINE OF CIVIC SPIRIT
- The sense of common purpose and solidarity in society is seen to be weakening, though there are signs of hope.
- Sign of hope: in Ireland during the nineties the social partners (employers, unions, farmers, community groups and the Government) achieved wage agreements so the whole community would benefit - an exercise in sacrifice and compromise for the common good.
- But the gap between rich and poor appears to be rising in Ireland and worldwide, and it is harder to get volunteers for community activities.
- 'Eclipse of the public': a name for this weakening of a sense of the common good.

CHALLENGES: UTILITARIANISM
- Utilitarianism: "The right action is the one that will ensure the greatest good for the greatest number of people."
- It looks like the common good: every action is judged by how it affects people, aiming at the happiness of as many as possible.
- But strict utilitarianism ignores the rights of individuals if their good stops the good of the majority. It is a question of numbers: majority rules, even if individual rights are trampled.
- Most modern accounts of the common good respect the rights of the person and seek the participation of all.

IRISH CIVIL LAW AND THE COMMON GOOD
- Eamon de Valera, Dail debates on the Constitution (3 June 1937): the legislature must work in the public interest and see that "the rights of the individual, as an individual, and the rights of a community, as a community, do not conflict and properly coordinate."
- Supreme Court (In re Article 26 and the Offences against the State (Amendment) Bill, 1940): "It seems difficult for us to understand how the dignity and freedom of the individual member of a State can be attained unless the social order is maintained in that State."
- So the common good and the personal good are interlinked and interdependent - similar to Plato's thought.
- Personal (fundamental) rights are protected in Articles 40-44 of the Constitution; some argue they derive from natural law. But they are not always absolute and are balanced with the common good.
- Court rulings show the strength of the common good argument can vary over time and circumstance.

CASE 1: THE DERRYNAFLAN HOARD - PUBLIC OWNERSHIP AND PERSONAL RIGHTS
- One of the most significant finds ever for Irish heritage.
- Found on Derrynaflan Island, County Tipperary, by a Mr Webb and his son on 17 February 1980.
- Buried eighteen inches underground near the site of an old church.
- Contained a chalice, a strainer and a stand, enclosed in a bronze basin. Made of silver, eighth-century early medieval Celtic design. Now in the National Museum in Dublin.
- The finders were trespassing at the time. They surrendered it to the National Museum expecting full compensation.
- The Court found that the common good of the State - its right of ownership of national treasure - was a higher value than the rights of the finders.
- As a matter of good will the finders were given 25,000 pounds.

CASE 2: NOEL AND MARIE MURRAY - PRISON AND CONJUGAL RIGHTS
- Serving life sentences for the murder of a Garda.
- They argued that under the Constitution they had the right to marry and have children, so should be allowed conjugal visits in prison.
- The Supreme Court held this right was subservient to the common good of the community to be protected from dangerous criminals.
- Prisoners lose various rights (e.g. the right to vote). Marriage rights depend on the person being free to carry them out. They lost the case.

CASE 3: BARBATO BORZA - COMPULSORY PURCHASE ORDER
- Bought a shop in Tallaght town centre in early 1988 for about 47,000 euro.
- In 1997 Dublin County Council placed a compulsory purchase order on it. A valuer estimated it worth about 127,000 euro.
- The Council took possession; the unit was vandalised and, after pressure from the residents' association, blocked up.
- The building was demolished, part used for road widening, and most sold to a property developer for "a profit of millions" according to Mr Borza.
- In August 2001 he received a letter under the Derelict Sites Act (1990) offering him 6,348 euro unconditionally. He refused and has received nothing.
- Raises the question of what happened to the balance of the common good and individual rights.

ASSIGNMENT CASES (PERSONAL RIGHTS VS COMMON GOOD)
- Torture to discover details of a terrorist threat; internment without trial of suspected terrorists; compulsory purchase orders for roads; avoiding tax by living outside the jurisdiction; police chasing a speeding stolen car in a residential area.

SUMMARY
- We all hold values as individuals and communities; these are often shared, but sometimes personal and community values clash.
- The concept of the common good has been present throughout history, from ancient Greece to the modern State. Christianity used the concept.
- John Paul II called people to value the virtue of solidarity.
- The common good seeks to avoid the extremes of individualism and totalitarianism.
- Irish civil law seeks to protect the common good while also protecting the rights of the individual.

KEY TERMS
- Personal values: qualities an individual considers good and important (e.g. health, freedom).
- Community values: values that seek the good of the whole community (e.g. right to education).
- The Common Good: what is best for the whole of society; shared by all and sought for the fulfilment of all.
- Pluralism: the existence of many different beliefs in one society.
- Utilitarianism: the right action ensures the greatest good for the greatest number.
- Individualism: selfishness and lack of care for others.
- Totalitarianism: putting the good of the State above the good of the person.

rows.prompt: Give one example of a conflict between a personal value and a community value, and suggest how it could be balanced.
rows.model_answer: People are free to listen to whatever music they like, but their neighbours have a right to sleep. Civil law balances one person's right to party with another's right to sleep, so music must not disturb neighbours in the middle of the night.

rows.prompt: Define the common good in your own words.
rows.model_answer: The common good is what is best for the whole of society. 'Common' means shared by everyone in the community, and 'good' means a goal sought for fulfilment. It encourages people to cooperate so shared goals are achieved for the fulfilment of all.

rows.prompt: Outline Aristotle's view of the common good.
rows.model_answer: Aristotle saw the human person as by nature a social and political being whose happiness comes from the public virtues of citizenship. He said political society exists for noble actions, not mere companionship. The good of the city is greater and 'nobler and more divine' than the good of one person.

rows.prompt: Name the two extremes that Christianity rejects in relation to the common good and explain each.
rows.model_answer: Christianity rejects individualism, which is selfishness and lack of care for others, because we are called to live in community and love our neighbour. It also rejects totalitarianism, which puts the good of the State above the person, as in Nazi Germany.

rows.prompt: What are the two complementary interpretations of the common good in Catholic teaching today?

rows.prompt: Name two difficulties in agreeing a common good today.

rows.prompt: Describe utilitarianism and explain how it differs from the common good.
rows.model_answer: Utilitarianism says the right action is the one that ensures the greatest good for the greatest number. Strictly followed, it ignores individuals' rights if they block the good of the majority. Modern accounts of the common good, by contrast, respect the rights of the person and seek the participation of all.

rows.prompt: Trace the development of the idea of the common good from ancient Greece and Rome to Christianity. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The beginnings of a common good theory are found in Plato's The Republic: 'The goal of the ideal state is not the advantage of any one class but the greatest possible happiness of the city as a whole.' A fair tax system that shares wealth is an example. Classical Greece saw the polis, the city state, as the place of human flourishing; the individual was private and incomplete, and the State was more important than the person. Aristotle saw the human person as by nature social and political, finding happiness in the public virtues of citizenship. He said 'Political society exists for the sake of noble actions, and not of mere companionship', and that securing the good for a nation is 'nobler and more divine' than for one person. In Rome, Cicero described a commonwealth (res publica) as people 'associated in agreement with respect to justice and a partnership for the common good'. The idea continued in republicanism and in Machiavelli and Rousseau. Christianity built on this through the command to love one's neighbour as oneself, which demands commitment to the common good. But it added that a person's final good lies in following God's plan; complete happiness is with God, not the State. Christianity rejects individualism, since we are called to community, and totalitarianism, which puts the State above the person, as in Nazi Germany. A person's freedom and dignity are achieved in communion with others.

Must show development across periods.

rows.prompt: With reference to two cases you have studied, show how Irish civil law balances individual rights with the common good. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Irish law tries to balance the rights of the individual with the common good. Eamon de Valera told the Dáil in 1937 that the legislature must make sure the rights of the individual and of the community 'do not conflict and properly coordinate'. In 1940 the Supreme Court said it is hard to see how individual dignity and freedom can exist 'unless the social order is maintained'. Personal rights are protected in Articles 40-44, but they are not absolute. In the Derrynaflan Hoard case, Mr Webb and his son found an eighth-century silver chalice, strainer and stand in a bronze basin on Derrynaflan Island, Co. Tipperary, on 17 February 1980. They were trespassing, but handed the treasure to the National Museum expecting full compensation. The Court found that the State's right to own its national treasure was a higher value than the rights of the finders, though they were given £25,000 as good will. In the case of Noel and Marie Murray, two prisoners serving life sentences for murdering a Garda, they claimed a constitutional right to marry and have children, and so to conjugal visits. The Supreme Court held this right was subservient to the common good of protecting the community from dangerous criminals; prisoners lose some rights, such as the vote, and marriage rights depend on being free to carry them out. Both cases show the common good can outweigh personal rights, though how strongly can vary over time.

rows.prompt: 'It is no longer possible to agree on a common good in modern society.' Discuss. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: There are real challenges to the common good today. The first is diversity. John Rawls says it is impossible to agree on a common good when so many different goods are sought. Pluralism, the existence of many different beliefs in one society, can make life interesting or be a source of fear, but it makes a shared vision harder. Some argue the only shared vision left is tolerance of every view, putting respect for the person above the common good. The second challenge is a decline in civic spirit. The gap between rich and poor seems to be rising, in Ireland and worldwide, and it is harder to find volunteers; some call this the 'eclipse of the public'. A third danger is utilitarianism, which looks at the greatest good for the greatest number but can trample individual rights. However, there are signs of hope. Others believe diversity can help us see more clearly what binds us together, since 'we can know a good in common that we cannot know alone'. In Ireland in the nineties the social partners agreed wage deals through sacrifice and compromise for the common good. Worldwide, the EU and UN work for the common good of humanity on fair trade, the environment, famine and refugees, alongside groups like Concern, Trócaire and Amnesty International. Catholic teaching also gives a clear guide: the common good must allow full participation of everyone and respect personal rights. So agreement is harder, but not impossible.

rows.prompt: Outline what the Second Vatican Council taught about the common good in Gaudium et spes. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: At the Second Vatican Council the Church spoke about people becoming more selfish. Gaudium et spes 30 says no one can 'wallow in the luxury of a merely individualistic morality'. The best way to fulfil obligations of justice and love is 'to contribute to the common good according to one's means and the needs of others'. It criticised those who boast of noble sentiments but do not care about society's needs, those who use fraud and cheating to avoid paying just taxes, and those who ignore social norms such as public hygiene and speed limits, endangering lives. It said everyone should consider social obligations a 'sacred duty'. Catholic teaching today says the common good must allow full participation of everyone and respect personal rights and duties.
